title: Who Keeps the Archive?
paragraphs: Leopold von Ranke, the nineteenth century German historian, famously urged historians to show the past as it actually was. The phrase is often quoted as if it were naive, but Ranke was arguing against a specific habit: treating history chiefly as a source of moral lessons. His insistence on archives and original documents helped shape the modern discipline.

Yet archives are not neutral either. Someone decided which letters were kept and which were burned, which voices were recorded and which were never written down at all. A historian who reads only what survives may reproduce, with impeccable footnotes, the priorities of the people who did the preserving. The bias, in such cases, lies not in the method but upstream of it.

In the early nineteen sixties, E. H. Carr pushed the point further. In his book What Is History?, he compared facts to fish swimming in a vast ocean: what the historian catches depends partly on chance, but mainly on where he chooses to fish and what tackle he uses. On this view, selection is not a regrettable lapse from objectivity; it is the very thing that turns a heap of facts into history.

The danger is that this insight can be stretched into something Carr did not intend. If every account is merely one perspective, then a careful study of census records and a piece of wartime propaganda become equally valid stories, and the historian's training counts for nothing. Carr himself resisted that slide, observing that a mountain which looks different from different angles does not therefore have no shape, or infinitely many.

What emerges is a discipline that is neither a mirror nor a mere opinion. Perspective cannot be removed, but it can be declared, tested against evidence and corrected by other historians working from other archives. The familiar slogan that history is written by the victors, repeated so often that few pause to ask who first said it, captures only half of this: the victors write first, but they rarely write last.

sources.claim: Leopold von Ranke 19. yüzyıl Alman tarihçisidir; geçmişi gerçekte olduğu gibi gösterme ilkesi ve arşivlere/özgün belgelere dayanması modern tarih disiplinini etkiledi; ilkeyi geçmişi yargılayıp gelecek için ders verme iddiasına karşı koydu.
E. H. Carr'ın What Is History? kitabı 1961'de yayımlanan derslerine dayanır.

Carr olguları okyanusta yüzen balıklara benzetir (tarihçinin yakaladığı kısmen şansa, esas olarak nerede ve hangi takımla avlandığına bağlıdır) ve farklı açılardan farklı görünen bir dağın biçimsiz ya da sonsuz biçimli olmadığını söyleyerek aşırı göreceliği reddeder.
